prompt: Design a production-grade Ceph operating model serving OpenStack RBD. Cover client/data contracts, releases and deployment method, cephx and maps, monitors/managers/OSDs/BlueStore, pools/PGs/CRUSH, replicated and erasure-coded policies, networks, capacity/fullness, performance, scrub/integrity, failure/recovery/backfill, RBD/OpenStack ownership, observability, hardware lifecycle, backups/disaster recovery, upgrades, cost, governance, incident response, exact cleanup and refusal conditions.
directAnswer: Start with client operations and data durability/latency/recovery contracts, then model Ceph as epoch-versioned maps plus decentralized client-to-OSD I/O. Monitors own map quorum; managers provide operational modules; OSD/BlueStore own object/shard persistence. Bind pool application and protection policy to a CRUSH rule whose logical buckets match physical power/network failure domains. Calculate eligible usable capacity after replication or K+M overhead, uneven fullness, thresholds, declared failure and movement reserve. Track PG availability, cleanliness and integrity separately. Design public/cluster networks and foreground/recovery queues from measured workloads. Scrub and repair are evidence-driven integrity workflows, not automatic proof. RBD/OpenStack identity must join service request, pool/image, locks/watchers, objects/PGs/OSDs and one writer. Use scoped cephx, protected keyrings and encrypted boundaries where required. Upgrade only by the exact supported release/deployment procedure with version inventory, health prechecks, canary, pause/abort and user/data validation. Refuse ambiguous FSID/release/object authority, correlated placement, unsafe min_size, full/backfill risk, unfenced writers, destructive repair, incompatible versions or missing cleanup.
foundation: Object identity maps to a PG; the current CRUSH rule and map compute an up set, while peering establishes an acting set and primary. Client writes are coordinated by the primary and persisted according to pool protection semantics. Maps, daemon status, PG state, media state and user I/O are different evidence boundaries.
reasoningSteps: Define client operations, durability, consistency, latency, throughput, RPO/RTO and data-owner contracts.
Inventory exact Ceph release, deployment method, hardware, clients, OpenStack releases and compatibility.
Design FSID/config authority, cephx entities/capabilities, key distribution, rotation and audit.
Place odd monitor quorum across independent latency-appropriate failure domains and protect clocks.
Separate monitor map authority from manager modules and dashboards.
Map each OSD to host, device, class, BlueStore block/DB/WAL, network and failure domain.
Define pools by application, object behavior, protection, size/min_size or K+M profile and quota.
Select replicated versus erasure coding from workload operations, overhead, latency and recovery cost.
Make CRUSH hierarchy/rules match physical power, rack, network and site independence.
Plan PG autoscaling and count from pool demand, balance, peering cost and daemon resources.
Trace object hash to PG, up/acting set, primary, shards and media acknowledgement.
Define public and cluster network bandwidth, MTU, failure and congestion evidence.
Measure foreground queues, media latency, commit/apply and replication/recovery contention.
Schedule scrub/deep-scrub with backlog, integrity, workload and repair decision controls.
Interpret each PG state component and acting history before recovery or repair.
Calculate raw, CRUSH-eligible, amplified, MAX AVAIL and failure/movement-reserved capacity.
Alert before nearfull/backfillfull/full using trends and time-to-exhaustion.
Define OSD add, drain, replace and destroy gates with safe-to-remove and cleanup proof.
Bound recovery/backfill with progress and user SLI, never disabling protection indefinitely.
Join OpenStack request/volume/image to cephx client, RBD pool/image/snapshot/clone/lock/watcher.
Require fencing before moving RBD writer authority or breaking a lock.
Back up monitor/control identity, configs, keys and application metadata; prove data recovery separately.
Upgrade by documented adjacency, minimum client/OSD releases, canary and pause/rollback limits.
Correlate FSID, epoch, pool/object/PG/OSD/client and user evidence without leaking keys or data.
Govern hardware, capacity, energy, data lifecycle, multi-tenancy, incident learning and exact cleanup.
seniorAnswer: I design Ceph from a user I/O and data-loss contract backward. Mon quorum supplies authoritative maps, not a centralized data path. The client computes placement; PG peering and an acting primary coordinate OSD/BlueStore persistence under a pool-specific protection policy. I prove physical CRUSH independence, eligible capacity and movement reserve, distinguish active from clean and consistent, and keep recovery bounded by both progress and user SLOs. OpenStack records never overrule RBD locks/watchers or OSD data, and no writer moves before fencing. Every change is release-specific, canaried and reversible within a declared boundary.
weakAnswer: Deploy three monitors, three replicas, many OSDs, enable the dashboard and alert whenever health is not OK.
whyWeak: It omits client/data contracts, physical failure domains, pool/min_size or K+M semantics, PG/acting history, eligible capacity/fullness, network/media bottlenecks, integrity, writer authority, RBD/OpenStack correlation, upgrades, recovery and cleanup.

evidence.signal: Versioned physical and logical topology plus CRUSH simulation
evidence.proves: Reviewed placement under declared maps and failures
evidence.doesNotProve: Media durability or unmodeled correlated failures

evidence.proves: Covered map, acting set, acknowledgement and state transitions

evidence.signal: Fenced RBD/OpenStack recovery with data invariant

evidence.proves: Observed supported transition for covered versions

followUps.prompt: Why are monitors not in the normal data path?
followUps.answer: Clients obtain maps from monitors and then communicate directly with OSDs; monitor quorum remains essential for authoritative map evolution.
The observed PGs are available and have configured placement complete at that time; it does not prove application semantics, all-object integrity, latency or disaster recovery.

followUps.prompt: How do replicated and erasure-coded pools differ operationally?
followUps.answer: They trade raw overhead, operation support, CPU/network/latency, shard count, small-I/O behavior and recovery amplification; exact suitability is workload and release dependent.

followUps.prompt: Why is MAX AVAIL more useful than raw free?
followUps.answer: It incorporates pool placement/protection and the limiting eligible devices, while raw free ignores CRUSH eligibility, amplification and imbalance.
